usage: the single most common '머리' complaint; 가 marks the body part
하다 sense of 'hair'; say this at a salon, not 머리카락을 자르다
감다 is the dedicated verb for hair only, never 씻다
fixed idiom 'good head' = clever; opposite is 머리가 나쁘다
examples: survival sentence; learn 가 + 아프다 as one chunk
here 머리 = hair; the adjective 길다 forces the 'hair' reading
I got a haircut and dyed it at the salon too.
real situation; 자르다 + 염색하다 are the salon collocations
nuance: 머리 covers both the head and the hair on it, and only context (the verb or adjective) tells them apart: 머리가 아프다 = head hurts, but 머리가 길다 / 머리를 감다 = hair. The strict word for a single strand is 머리카락, yet in speech Koreans almost always shorten it to 머리, so 'cut my hair' is 머리를 자르다, not 머리카락을 자르다. The pitfall for English speakers is the washing verb: hair takes 감다 (머리를 감다), never the 씻다 you use for hands or face, so 머리를 씻다 sounds childish or wrong. Also note 머리가 좋다/나쁘다 is a fixed idiom for being smart/dim, not a comment on hair quality, and the body part is always marked with 가 (머리가 아파요), not 을.

usage: common complaint; 가 marks the body part
감다 here means 'close', distinct from washing hair
examples: survival sentence; 눈 stays singular even for both eyes
My older sister has really big eyes.
My eyesight is bad so I go around wearing glasses.
real situation; 눈이 나쁘다 + 안경을 쓰다 collocate
nuance: 눈 is the eye, but the identical spelling also means 'snow'; the two are split by pitch (eye = short/low, snow = long/high) and above all by context, so listeners rarely confuse them. Korean treats the pair of eyes as one uncountable 눈, so you never pluralize it. The big English-speaker trap is eyesight: vision is rated with 좋다 (good) and 나쁘다 (bad) — 눈이 좋아요 / 눈이 나빠요 — never with 'strong/weak' (강하다/약하다), which would sound bizarre. Note that 눈을 감다 uses the same 감다 as washing hair but means 'close', and the related verb 보다 ('see/look') is what the eye does, while 만나다 ('meet') is for people, so don't blend them.

usage: the standard cold symptom; 막히다 = be blocked
for snot use the compound 콧물 (코+물), not just 코
풀다 'release'; never 코를 불다 (that is whistling/blowing air)
to have a high nose bridge
examples: survival sentence; learn 막히다 as the blocked-nose verb
I keep having a runny nose because of a cold.
everyday; 콧물 + 나다 is the runny-nose collocation
Blowing your nose with a tissue is the polite thing to do.
real situation; 코를 풀다 = blow nose
nuance: 코 is the nose, but cold symptoms split into precise collocations English speakers must memorize: a blocked nose is 코가 막히다 (막히다 = be blocked) and a runny nose is 콧물이 나다, where 콧물 literally stitches 코(nose)+물(water) into 'nose-water' = snot. Saying 코가 아프다 actually means the nose physically hurts (an injury), so it does NOT convey a cold — that is the classic 직역 trap. To blow your nose is 코를 풀다 (풀다 'to release/undo'); beware 코를 불다, which means to blow air out like a whistle and sounds absurd here. For looks, a tall nose bridge (admired in Korea) is 코가 높다, with 코가 낮다 as the flat-bridge opposite, paralleling how 키가 크다 works for height.

usage: 벌리다 = spread apart; what the dentist asks
fixed food idiom, not literal 'fits in mouth'
idiom 'short mouth'; eats little or fussily
examples: survival sentence; 벌리다 is the open-mouth verb
This kimchi stew really suits my taste.
everyday; 입에 맞다 judges flavor, not size
우리 아이는 입이 짧아서 골고루 안 먹어요.
My kid is a picky eater so doesn't eat a variety.
real situation; 입이 짧다 = fussy eater
nuance: 입 is the mouth, but its most useful expressions are idioms that won't survive word-for-word translation. 입에 맞다 means food 'suits your taste' (lit. 'fits the mouth') — it judges flavor, so 'this fits in my mouth' is a beginner mistranslation. 입이 짧다 ('short mouth') describes a picky or light eater, while 입이 무겁다 ('heavy mouth') means tight-lipped/discreet and 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth') means a blabbermouth — none are about physical size. To physically open the mouth is 입을 벌리다 (벌리다 = spread apart), as a dentist commands; do not use 열다 ('open' a door/box) for the mouth. Note also that 입 (mouth, the organ) is different from 말 (speech/words), so 'watch your mouth' as in language is 말조심하다, not anything with 입.

usage: body complaint; 가 marks the part
to not be able to hear
uses passive 들리다, not active 듣다
examples: It was so loud I covered my ears.
할머니는 귀가 어두우셔서 크게 말씀드려야 해요.
Grandma is hard of hearing so I have to speak loudly to her.
real situation; 귀가 어둡다 + honorific 말씀드리다
nuance: 귀 is the ear, and the key English-speaker pitfall is the verb of hearing. Korean splits 듣다 (to listen actively, by choice) from 들리다 (to be heard / reach the ear, passively, beyond control). So 'I can't hear' is 귀가 안 들려요 with the passive 들리다 — using 못 듣다 implies you deliberately didn't listen, which is rude when talking about someone's deafness. There are two natural ways to describe hard-of-hearing: the plain 귀가 안 들리다 and the gentler idiom 귀가 어둡다 ('the ear is dark'), whose opposite 귀가 밝다 ('bright ear') means keen hearing. To plug your ears against noise is 귀를 막다 (막다 = block), the same 막다 as a blocked nose (코가 막히다). When speaking about elders, pair this with honorifics, e.g. 귀가 어두우세요.

usage: 씻다 for hands, never the 감다 used for hair
잡다 = grasp; romantic or to lead a child
idiom 'hand goes'; a fussy task or needy child
idiom 'big hand'; cooks/gives a lot, not literal size
examples: hygiene basic; 씻다 is the hand-washing verb
길을 건널 때 아이 손을 꼭 잡으세요.
Hold the child's hand tightly when crossing the street.
우리 엄마는 손이 커서 항상 음식을 많이 하세요.
My mom is generous so she always cooks a lot of food.
nuance: 손 is the hand, and the first thing to fix is the washing verb: hands take 씻다 (손을 씻다), in deliberate contrast to hair, which uses 감다 — mixing them (손을 감다) is a classic beginner slip. Beyond the literal organ, 손 powers vivid idioms that aren't about anatomy: 손이 크다 ('big hand') means generous, especially someone who cooks or gives a lot, not someone with large hands; 손이 가다 ('the hand goes') means a task or person takes a lot of effort/attention; and 손이 모자라다 ('hands are short') means short-staffed. To hold someone's hand is 손을 잡다 (잡다 = grasp), used both romantically and to guide a child across the road. Note the hand is usually the object of an action, so it pairs with 을/를 (손을 씻다, 손을 잡다) rather than 가.

usage: idiom 'wide foot' = well-connected, not big feet
examples: survival sentence; common after a long walk
I fell on the stairs and hurt my foot.
everyday; 다치다 takes 을/를: 발을 다치다
그 사람은 발이 넓어서 모르는 사람이 없어요.
He is so well-connected he knows everyone.
real situation; 발이 넓다 = socially connected
nuance: 발 is specifically the foot — the part below the ankle — and Korean keeps it strictly separate from 다리 (the leg, the whole limb above), so pointing at your ankle and saying 다리 is wrong; that is the core mix-up for English speakers who blur 'leg/foot'. Useful collocations: 발을 다치다 (injure the foot, with 다치다 taking 을/를) and 발이 붓다 (the foot swells), where 붓다 is a ㅅ-irregular verb that drops ㅅ before a vowel → 부어요, 부었어요, not 붓어요. Idiomatically 발이 넓다 ('wide foot') means well-connected with a broad social network, never literally big feet (for that you'd say 발이 크다). When you cause an injury yourself, prefer the active 다치다 (발을 다쳤어요) over a passive construction.

usage: the everyday stomachache; also idiom for jealousy
fixed phrase; 고프다 is ㅡ-irregular: 고파요
fixed phrase; 부르다 is 르-irregular: 불러요
examples: survival sentence; the go-to stomachache line
everyday; spoken as one word 배고파요
I ate a lot so I'm full.
nuance: 배 means the belly/stomach (the body region), and the same syllable also means 'pear' and 'boat/ship' — three homonyms split only by context. Hunger and fullness are locked set phrases that ALWAYS keep 배: 배가 고프다 (hungry) and 배가 부르다 (full); you cannot say 나는 고파요 alone, which is the top beginner error. Both adjectives are irregular: 고프다 is ㅡ-irregular (고파요, 고팠어요) and 부르다 is 르-irregular (불러요, 불렀어요). Note 배 here is the colloquial stomach for aches and hunger, distinct from the Sino-Korean 위 (胃, the actual stomach organ) used in medical contexts like 위염 (gastritis). A culturally important idiom: 배가 아프다 also figuratively means to be jealous of someone's good fortune ('my stomach hurts' = green with envy), so context decides literal pain vs. envy.

usage: from sitting too long; pins and needles
examples: survival sentence; common after standing long
everyday; 다리가 길다 describes the limb
My leg went numb from sitting so long.
nuance: 다리 is the leg — the whole limb from hip to ankle — and must be kept apart from 발 (the foot only); calling the foot 다리 is the classic English-speaker error since English loosely says 'leg'. The same word 다리 also means 'bridge' (the structure), identical in spelling, separated only by context — 다리를 건너다 = cross a bridge, 다리가 아프다 = my leg hurts. Common collocations: 다리를 다치다 (injure the leg, 다치다 taking 을/를) and 다리가 저리다, where 저리다 describes that tingly 'pins-and-needles / fallen asleep' feeling after sitting cross-legged too long. For looks, 다리가 길다 (long legs) is a strong compliment, mirroring 키가 크다 for height. Note a leg ache is marked with 가 (다리가 아파요), while an action done to the leg takes 을/를 (다리를 다쳤어요).

usage: the standard cold symptom, not just neck pain
fixed phrase; 마르다 is 르-irregular: 말라요
to lose one's voice / be hoarse
from shouting or a cold; 'the throat rests'
examples: survival sentence; usually means sore throat from a cold
Please give me some water, I'm thirsty.
I lost my voice from cheering.
real situation; 목이 쉬다 = go hoarse
nuance: 목 covers both the neck and the throat, so 목이 아프다 most often means a sore throat from a cold, NOT neck pain — assuming it only means 'neck' is the main English-speaker pitfall (for true neck/shoulder stiffness Koreans more often say 목이 뻐근하다 or specify 목덜미). Thirst is the fixed phrase 목이 마르다 ('the throat dries'), where 마르다 is 르-irregular → 말라요, 말랐어요; do not invent 목이 건조하다. A swollen throat is 목이 붓다 (ㅅ-irregular → 부어요), the same swelling verb as 발이 붓다, and going hoarse is 목이 쉬다 (lit. 'the throat rests'). Idiomatically 목이 빠지게 기다리다 means to wait so eagerly your neck stretches out ('wait with bated breath'). A throat/neck symptom marks the part with 가 (목이 아파요).

usage: take care not to catch cold
examples: survival sentence; memorize 에 걸리다 as one unit
Colds are going around these days.
Take care not to catch a cold, the weather got cold.
real situation; caring goodbye in winter
nuance: 감기 (感氣, 'feeling/affecting + air/energy') is the Sino-Korean word for a common cold, the everyday illness with cough, runny nose, and sore throat — distinct from the heavier 독감 (毒感, 'poison-cold' = influenza/the flu), which is a serious, feverish illness, so don't call the flu just 감기. The critical grammar point is the particle: you 'catch' a cold with 감기에 걸리다, using 에, because 걸리다 ('get caught by/hung on') takes a location-like target — 감기를 걸리다 with 을 is the number-one English-speaker error. Cold medicine is taken with 먹다 (감기약을 먹다, lit. 'eat medicine'), never 마시다 ('drink'), even for liquid syrup. The phrase 감기 조심하세요 ('be careful of cold') is a warm, very common parting line when the weather turns cold, much like 'stay warm / don't catch a cold.'

감기를 걸리다 with 을 is the number-one English-speaker error — 걸리다 requires 에, so it is 감기에 걸리다.

mistakes: Saying 감기를 걸리다 — 걸리다 requires the particle 에, so it is 감기에 걸리다.
Calling the flu 감기 — the flu is 독감 (a far more severe illness); 감기 is an ordinary cold.
Saying 감기약을 마시다 — medicine is 'eaten' in Korean, so use 감기약을 먹다 even for liquid medicine.

usage: fixed phrase; 나다 lit. '(it) comes out'
높다, not 크다, for fever level
examples: survival sentence; 열이 나다 is the core phrase
My child has a high fever so I'm worried.
After taking medicine the fever went down a bit.
real situation; 열이 내리다 = fever subsides
nuance: 열 (熱, the hanja for 'heat') is a fever, and the must-learn collocation is 열이 나다, where 나다 literally means '(something) comes out/arises' — Korean conceives a fever as heat 'coming out' of the body, so you never say 열을 가지다 ('have/possess a fever'), a direct translation of English 'have' that sounds completely unnatural. You can also say 열이 있다 ('there is fever') as a calmer alternative. The level of a fever is described with 높다/낮다 (열이 높다 = high fever), not 크다/작다, and once treated, 열이 내리다 ('the fever comes down') is the natural way to say it subsides — paralleling how prices or temperature 내리다. To take someone's temperature is 열을 재다 (재다 = to measure), the same verb as 키를 재다 (measure height). Don't confuse this 열 with the homonym 열 meaning 'ten' (열 개 = ten items); context separates them.

mistakes: Saying 열을 가지다 for having a fever — this English-style 'have' is unnatural; use 열이 나요 or 열이 있어요.
Describing a high fever as 열이 커요 — fever level uses 높다, so it is 열이 높아요.
